passage: I'm Ankita, and last term my friend Keerthana changed so fast it scared me. She quit chess club, which she loved. She stopped sitting with us at lunch. In the April heat she wore a full-sleeved sweater every day. Then she handed me her whole set of sketch pens and said, "Keep them. I won't need them." Some people in our class group chat were joking that she was being dramatic. I didn't add anything. After school I walked home with her and said I'd noticed, and that I cared. She shrugged and said nothing was going to get better anyway. That scared me even more. I went straight back to school and found Ms Fernandes, our class teacher. She listened, thanked me, and phoned Keerthana's parents and the school counsellor before I'd even left the staffroom. Keerthana is getting help now. We're still friends.

qa.q: What did Keerthana give Ankita?
qa.a: Her whole set of sketch pens.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana's shrug and words scare Ankita even more?
qa.a: Saying nothing was going to get better sounded hopeless, so Ankita feared Keerthana might be in real danger.

qa.q: Which choice did Ankita make instead of joining the group-chat jokes?

Coach's note, under-16 hockey squad, Tuesday. Coach Raghav.
For three weeks Jaya has skipped the warm-up jokes she usually leads and sat alone on the bench. Today she was suddenly bright and calm, and after practice she handed her new stick to a junior and said, "You'll use it more than me." She also had a bandaged wrist she wouldn't explain. Two players were whispering about it; I told them to stop, and to come to me whenever they're worried about a teammate.
What I did next: I asked Jaya to help me carry cones, and in the storeroom I told her what I'd noticed. I asked plainly whether she was thinking of hurting herself. She was quiet, then said, "Sometimes." I stayed with her, thanked her for telling me, and phoned the school counsellor, who came over within the hour. Her mother arrived soon after, and they went together to the counsellor's office.

qa.q: What did Jaya hand to a junior?
qa.a: Her new stick.

qa.q: What worried Raghav about Jaya's sudden brightness?
qa.a: Raghav felt worried because, after three weeks of withdrawal, the sudden calm and giving away her new stick felt to Raghav like warning signs, not recovery.

passage: The skate park in Auckland was nearly empty when Kaito sat down on the ramp beside his friend Paulo and said, without looking up, "I've been hurting myself. Don't tell anyone. Promise." Paulo's stomach dropped, but he kept his voice steady. "Thanks for telling me. That took guts." He listened while Kaito talked about the pressure at home and the nights he couldn't sleep. Then Paulo said, "I can't promise to keep this secret, because I care whether you're safe. Are you safe right now?" Kaito said he wasn't planning anything tonight, but he was tired of everything. Paulo didn't leave him. They walked together to Paulo's house, where Paulo's dad switched off the TV, listened, and told Kaito it wasn't his fault he was struggling. With Kaito beside him, he phoned Kaito's mother and then a youth helpline that same evening.

passage:
Vikas beta,
I'm writing because when I try to say this aloud, my voice shakes.
Yesterday, when I found the bandages in your drawer and you told me why, I panicked. I shouted, I took your phone, I said things like "How could you do this to us?" That was my fear talking, and it was wrong. You were hurting, and I made it about me. I'm sorry.
Here is what I know now. I'm not angry with you. I'm scared, and I feel guilty that I didn't see how bad things were. None of that is yours to fix.
Last night, once calmer, I rang a parents' helpline. This morning I phoned the school counsellor. She gave us the name of a psychologist who works with teenagers, and we have an appointment on Thursday. I can come in with you, or wait outside, whichever you choose.
Your phone is back on your desk.
Love always,
Mummy (Alka)

qa.a: Alka feels scared, guilty for not seeing how bad things were, and sorry for shouting.

"I'll try. I'm right here."

passage: I'm Sabina, and I'm writing this a year on. Last winter my job ended and my grandmother fell ill in the same month. The pain felt too big for one body. I started hurting myself when it got unbearable, because for a little while afterwards I felt quiet and numb. Then shame would flood in, and I'd hide it under long sleeves and jokes. Ojas, who shared my desk at the office, noticed me flinch when he bumped my arm. He didn't lecture or look disgusted. He said, "Whatever's going on, you don't deserve to be punished for it. Can I help you find someone to talk to?" He stayed with me that afternoon, sat beside me while I called my sister, and we booked a doctor before we left the office. Later I began seeing a psychologist. Some nights the urge still comes. Now I call Ojas or my sister instead, and we talk until it passes.

qa.a: Sabina's job ended and Sabina's grandmother fell ill in the same month.

Monday. Neelam hadn't come to the mess for two days. At night she lay facing the wall and barely answered. Baljeet, her roommate, lay awake, afraid that asking about dark thoughts would put the idea in her head.
Tuesday. After class Neelam said, half-joking, "It'd be easier for everyone if I just vanished." Baljeet closed the door at once, sat down beside her and asked, "Are you thinking of hurting yourself, or of ending your life?" Neelam's eyes filled. "Yes. Nobody's asked me that." Her shoulders dropped, as if she had put down something heavy. Baljeet stayed with her, asked her to hand over anything she might use to hurt herself, and gave it to the warden. Together they called the crisis line, which linked them to the campus counsellor that evening.
Friday. Neelam was back in the mess, tired but eating. "When you asked me straight out," she told Baljeet, "I could finally breathe."

passage: Sit, Ira, the tea's still hot. You asked why I always ask patients the hard question so plainly. I've been Preeti the nurse on this ward for thirty years, so here is the reason. When I was nineteen, my hostel friend Shobha gave away her favourite books and said, "Don't waste your time on me." Everyone warned me not to mention suicide, that it would give her ideas. I was terrified. But one night I sat on her bed and said, "Shobha, are you thinking of ending your life?" She burst into tears and said yes, and then, "Thank God someone asked." I didn't leave her side. I asked the warden to lock away anything that could hurt her, and we went to the hospital emergency together that same night. Shobha is sixty now, with three grandchildren. So when a young person looks like that, I ask. The question won't put the thought there. Silence is what's dangerous. Now drink your tea, and then go and ask Room Six.

qa.a: Her favourite books.

"Reena, you've been watching that kettle for five minutes."
"Sorry. Just tired. Afreen, can I ask something weird? If I weren't around, the team would manage fine, right?"

You asked on the phone why I sound so flat. I'll try to answer here, because writing is easier than saying it.
For about three months I've been waking at four with my heart racing, dreading school. I haven't told anyone, for a whole list of reasons. Achan says counsellors are for people who can't manage their own minds. I worry it costs a lot, and Amma is already counting every rupee. Mostly, I tell myself it isn't bad enough. I still go to class. I still smile in photos.
But a senior at school waited until she couldn't leave the house at all. I don't want to wait that long.
Our school counsellor is free. When you're home next Saturday, will you come with me, and help me tell Amma and Achan?
Gopika

passage: Jahnavi, since this podcast is about asking for help, here's why I waited so long. I'm Farida, and I kept a list of excuses. First: people would call me weak. Class teacher's note, 9B, Wednesday. Jomon.
At the end of the day, while I was packing test papers, Divyansh hovered at my desk. "Sir, can I talk to you? It's kind of serious." My first instinct was to say, "Tomorrow, I'm late." I'm glad I didn't. He told me he hasn't slept properly for weeks, that his chest tightens every morning at the school gate, and that he's scared his parents will think he's making excuses for his marks. I put the papers down and said, "Thank you for telling me. That took courage." I gave him no speech about studying harder.
What I did next: I walked him to the school counsellor's room before she left, and with his permission I phoned his mother, who came in that evening. As he left, Divyansh asked if he could come back to me if it got worse. I said yes. I think he will.

Thursday night.
Pankaj stayed back after tabla class today, tuning and retuning the same drum. Then he said, very fast, "Tanvir Sir, I've been feeling really low for months and I don't know who to tell." My first thought was the old lecture I got at his age: focus, practise more, stop brooding. I swallowed it. I said, "Thank you for telling me. I'm glad you chose me."
He talked for a long while. He's skipping school some days, can't enjoy even music, and he's scared his father will call it drama. I didn't argue or promise it would pass by itself. I asked if we could call his mother together. We did, from my verandah, and she came to fetch him. She's booking the family doctor for tomorrow and asked me to come along if Pankaj wants.
Before he left he said, "Can I talk to you again if it gets bad?"
"Any time," I said.

Anirban came to my office hour today, not about his project. He said he has been sleeping badly for about five weeks, missed two lab submissions, and stopped calling home because "there's nothing good to report." Sunday, late
Made a list tonight because my head won't hold thoughts in order.
- About a month of waking up already exhausted.
- Missed three shifts at the bakery. Told my manager I had a fever. I didn't.

passage:
Subject: Re: how did you find your therapist?
Hi Urmila,
Of course I'll share. First, I ignored the short videos of life coaches promising to "fix anxiety in seven days". I looked for people who listed their qualifications and registration, and I asked my family doctor for two names.
The first therapist was qualified, but we just didn't click. I felt rushed, and I nearly gave up on therapy altogether. My sister said, "You wouldn't stop seeing doctors after one bad one." So I tried the second name. A much better fit.
Around the fourth session it got harder before it got easier. I wanted to quit. I'm glad I didn't.
One more thing, and I mean it: if you ever feel unsafe, don't wait for an appointment. Call a helpline or go to the emergency department that same day.
Proud of you for looking.

passage: Elizabeth, people always ask me how I "found the right person", as if it were luck. It wasn't. I'm Binita. When I moved to London for work at twenty-four, I was low for months. A colleague recommended a "healer" with no training who charged a fortune. I said no, and checked the professional register online instead. I tried two therapists before one felt right: someone who let me take my time and still challenged me. But the part I really want your listeners to hear is about one night in March, when my thoughts got frightening and I didn't feel safe. My next session was four days away. The old me would have waited. Instead I rang the crisis helpline, and they stayed on the phone while my flatmate took me to A&E. My therapist said later that was exactly the right call.
